[[ca:Shugendo]][[cs:Šugendó]][[de:Shugendō]][[en:Shugendō]][[es:Shugendō]][[fr:Shugendō]][[it:Shugendō]][[ja:修験道]][[ko:수험도]][[pl:Shugendō]][[pt:Shugendō]][[ru:Сюгэндо]][[simple:Shugendō]][[sk:Šugendó]][[sr:Šugendo]][[tr:Shugendō]][[zh:修驗道]] [[ca:Shugendo]][[cs:Šugendó]][[de:Shugendō]][[en:Shugendō]][[es:Shugendō]][[fr:Shugendō]][[it:Shugendō]][[ja:修験道]][[ko:수험도]][[pl:Shugendō]][[pt:Shugendō]][[ru:Сюгэндо]][[simple:Shugendō]][[sk:Šugendó]][[sr:Šugendo]][[tr:Shugendō]][[zh:修驗道]] {{Short description|Syncretic religion from Heian Japan}} {{Italic title}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} [[Image:立石光正DSCF0451.JPG|thumb|''Shugendō ''practitioners (''Shugenja'') in the mountains of {{ill|Kumano, Mie|en|Kumano, Mie|WD=Q819672|lt=Kumano, Mie|1=Kumano, Mie}}]] [[File:En no Gyōja, Kamakura period, polychromed wood.JPG|thumb|upright|Statue of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of ''Shugendo''. {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, c. 1300–1375, {{ill|Kimbell Art Museum|en|Kimbell Art Museum|WD=Q1741629|lt=Kimbell Art Museum|1=Kimbell Art Museum}}.]] [[Image:Oominesanji stairs.jpg|thumb|upright|Stairs on the way to {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}}, the holy site of ''Shugendō''.]] [[Image:Fudō Myōō.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] silk scroll from [[Daigo-ji]] ({{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}), a major Shingon temple and Shugendō site.]] [[Image:Zao-Gongen-Kimpusen-Temple-Yoshino.jpg|thumb|upright|''Zaō Gongen'', a key deity in ''Shugendō'', in [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple.]] {{nihongo|'''''Shugendō'''''|||lit. the "Way [of] Trial [and] Practice", the "Way of ''Shugen'', or ''Gen''-practice"}} is a highly {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} religion,{{Cite journal |last=Sekimori |first=Gaynor |date=2009 |title=Defining Shugendō Past and Present: The "Restoration" of Shugendō at Nikkō and Koshikidake |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/asie_0766-1177_2009_num_18_1_1330 |journal=Cahiers d'Extrême-Asie |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=47–71 |doi=10.3406/asie.2009.1330}} a body of [[:en:Ascetic|Ascetic]] practices that originated in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period|1=Nara period}} of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}} having evolved during the 7th century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local [[Japanese folklore|folk-religious practices]], [[:en:Ko-shinto|Shinto]] {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} and [[Taoism]]. The final purpose of ''Shugendō'' is for practitioners to find supernatural power and save themselves and the masses by conducting religious training while treading through steep mountain ranges. Practitioners are called {{nihongo|''Shugenja''|}} or {{nihongo|''[[Yamabushi]]''|||literally "Mountain Prostrator"}}.{{Cite web|title=Exoteric Buddhism, Esoteric Buddhism, and Shugendo – 顕教・密教・修験道|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|url-status=live|website=www.tendai-jimon.jp|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}} The mountains where ''shugendo'' is practiced are all over Japan, and can span multiple mountains within one range such as the Ōmine mountain range with [[Mount Hakkyō]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} or the Ishizuchisan mountain range with [[:ja:%E7%93%B6%E3%83%B6%E6%A3%AE|Kamegamori]] and Tengudake. The ''Shugendō'' worldview includes a large pantheon of deities (which include Buddhist and Shinto figures). Some of the most important figures are the {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} figures of [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] and {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}}. Other key figures are {{nihongo|''[[Gongen]]''|}}, which are considered to be the manifestation of Buddhas as Japanese [[kami]]. {{nihongo|[[Zaō Gongen]]|}} is one of the most important gongen in ''Shugendō''.{{Cite web|title=修験道とは …「自然と人間」|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |title=The Formation and its Meaning of the 75-sacred-place View in the Omine Sacred Mountain Area |author=Masayasu Oda|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502160622/https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |accessdate=2 February 2021|archive-date=2 May 2019 }} == History == ''Shugendō'' evolved during the seventh century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local folk-religious practices, Shinto mountain worship and Buddhism.{{cite book|last1=Kornicki|first1=P.F.|last2=McMullen|first2=I. J.|title=Religion in Japan: Arrows to Heaven and Earth|date=1996|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0521550284|pages=13–|edition=Reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gsLDwvmnt_oC&pg=PA13|access-date=11 March 2017|language=en}} The seventh-century ascetic and mystic {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} is widely considered as the patriarch of ''Shugendō'', having first organized ''Shugendō'' as a doctrine. ''Shugendō'' literally means "the path of training and testing" or "the way to spiritual power through discipline."{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings|url=https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick|url-access=limited|date=1994|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Connecticut|isbn=0313264317|page=[https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick/page/n133 99]}}{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=Collected Writings of Carmen Blacker|date=2000|publisher=Japan Library|location=Richmond, Surrey|isbn=978-1873410929|pages=186–199|chapter=16: Initiation in the Shugendō: the Passage Through the Ten States of Existence}} ''Shugendō'' practitioners are also said to be descendants of the [[:en:Kōya Hijiri|Kōya Hijiri]] monks of the eighth and ninth centuries.{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|date=1999|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410859|edition=3rd|location=Richmond|pages=165–167}} From the ninth century, elements of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana Buddhism|1=Vajrayana}} such as {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} and {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Buddhism were taken into ''Shugendō'' and it developed further. In the Heian period, it became very popular among the nobles living in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to visit [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]] (three major shrines, [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]], [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] and [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]), which was the common holy place of ''Shugendō'', Shinto and Buddhism.{{Cite book|author=Makoto Satō, Fumihiko Gomi, Toshihiko Takano and Yasushi Toriumi|title=詳説日本史研究|year=2008|publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha Ltd.|isbn=978-4634011014}} The {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji|1=Meiji era}} government, which [[Shinbutsu bunri|erected a barrier between]] Shinto and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, ruled that ''Shugendō'' was unacceptable because of its amalgamation of the two religions, and officially forbade it in 1872. With the advent of {{ill|Freedom of religion in Japan|en|Freedom of religion in Japan|WD=Q5500773|lt=religious freedom in Japan|1=Freedom of religion in Japan}} after {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, ''Shugendō'' was revived.{{cite book|author=Catherine Cornille|title=The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Inter-Religious Dialogue|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHdgFhRKCOsC|year=2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1118529942}} In 1907, Yoshitaro Shibasaki and his team successfully climbed {{ill|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|en|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|WD=Q1109050|lt=Mount Tsurugi|1=Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)}}, which was regarded as the last unclimbed mountain in Japan. However, they found a metal cane decoration and a sword on the top of the mountain, and it turned out that someone had reached the top before them. A later scientific investigation revealed that the metal cane decoration and sword dated from the late Nara period to the early Heian period and that ''shugenja'' had climbed Mount Tsurugi more than 1,000 years ago.{{cite web|url=https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930190011/https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|script-title=ja:銅錫杖頭附鉄剣（剣岳発見）|language=ja|publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]], Government of Japan|archive-date=September 30, 2020}} The Ōmine mountain range, which stretches 100 km from north to south and connects {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} and [[Kumano Region|Kumano]], was historically the biggest practice place of ''Shugendō''. The highest peak of the Ōmine mountain range is [[Mount Hakkyō]] at an altitude of 1915 m, and there are 75 places for ascetic practices along the mountain trail, and {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}} Temple at the top of {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} at an altitude of 1719 m is considered to be the highest sacred site of ''Shugendō''. At present, the Ōmine mountain range is designated as a {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} {{ill|World Heritage Site|en|World Heritage Site|WD=Q9259|lt=World Heritage Site|1=World Heritage Site}} "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}" and {{ill|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|en|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|WD=Q1204533|lt=Yoshino-Kumano National Park|1=Yoshino-Kumano National Park}}. In modern times, ''Shugendō'' is practiced mainly through {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} and {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} temples. Some temples include {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kimpusen-ji|1=Kimpusen-ji}} in {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} (Tendai), Ideha Shrine in the {{ill|Three Mountains of Dewa|en|Three Mountains of Dewa|WD=Q1155726|lt=Three Mountains of Dewa|1=Three Mountains of Dewa}} and [[Daigo-ji]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} (Shingon). == Practices == According to Miyake Hitoshi, Shugend''ō'' rituals include "festivals, fortunetelling, divination, prayers and incantations, exorcism, spells, charms and so forth."Miyake Hitoshi. "Religious Rituals in Shugendo A Summary." ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 1989 16/2–3 Hitoshi describes the main worldview which informs Shugendo praxis as one which:
assumes the existence of at least two realms of existence, that of the daily lives of human beings, and a separate, supernatural spiritual realm behind, and which controls that of the daily lives of human beings. The mountains are seen either as a sacred space which is part of both of these worlds, or is seen to actually be a part of the spiritual world. The altar space during the fire ceremony, or the area of a matsuri, is also considered to be this kind of sacred space.
The {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} deity [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] (Sanskrit: Acala, "Immovable") plays a central role in the Shugendo cosmology practice. Another important Buddha is {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}} (大日如来，Mahavairocana). The Shugendo pantheon also includes numerous other Buddhist, Shinto and local religious figures. The most important Shugend''ō'' practices are "practices in the mountains" (''nyūbu shugyō'', 入峰修行). In Shugend''ō'', sacred mountains are seen as a supernatural home of numerous deities and as a symbol of the entire universe. According to Hitoshi, "the central element which forms both of these rituals is the symbolic action exhibited in a state of identification with the central deity Fudō Myōō." The main source of the shugenja's spiritual power generally understood to be Fudō Myōō and a shugenja gains the ability to use Fudō Myōō's power through mountain practices. There are three main forms of mountain practice according to Miyake Hitoshi: * "Entering the mountain to make offerings of flowers, read or bury sutras, and so forth, in honor of various buddhas or other deities, based on the belief that the mountain is a sacred area like a mandala." * "Entering the mountain for a certain period of time," a kind of mountain retreat during which yamabushi do various ascetic practices and receive esoteric knowledge and initiations. * The most severe and advanced ''nyūbu'' is the wintertime retreat in the mountains. This is said to confer special spiritual powers. Shugendō esoteric initiations are called ''shōkanjō'' (正灌頂) and are unique to Shugendō tradition (but are based on Vajrayana Buddhist {{ill|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|en|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|WD=Q3505394|lt=abhiseka|1=Empowerment (Vajrayana)}} ceremonies). Another important Shugendō practice is the demonstration of magical and spiritual powers (''genjutsu'', 験 術). Such displays may include fire walking, walking on swords, and entering boiling water. Yet another important religious practice in Shugendō is various rites or rituals of worship (''kuyōhō'', 供養法) which includes making offerings to Shugendō deities (such as Fudō Myōō and [[Gongen|Zaō Gongen]]) as well as the chanting of sutras. Shugendō practitioners also take part in [[Japanese festivals|Shinto festivals]] (matsuri, 祭) and make offerings to [[kami]]. Other practices which are part of Shugendō include the following: * {{ill|Fortune-telling|en|Fortune-telling|WD=Q8011595|lt=Fortunetelling|1=Fortune-telling}} and {{ill|Divination|en|Divination|WD=Q1043197|lt=Divination|1=Divination}} (''bokusen'') * obtaining {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=oracles|1=Oracle}} through {{ill|Mediumship|en|Mediumship|WD=Q25416928|lt=mediums|1=Mediumship}} (''fujutsu'') * obtaining oracles through mediums that have been possessed by a deity (''yori kitō'', 憑祈禱) * Fire ceremonies for averting misfortunes (''sokusai [[Homa (ritual)|goma]]''), usually focused around [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] * Using {{ill|Incantation|en|Incantation|WD=Q1999796|lt=incantations|1=Incantation}} (''kaji'') for a specific purpose * Spells and charms (''fuju, majinai''), used for healing, childbirth, protection and so on. These may be inscribed on {{ill|Amulet|en|Amulet|WD=Q131557|lt=amulets|1=Amulet}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism|1=Exorcism}} (''tsukimono otoshi'') for healing purposes Shugendo ritualists also practice different rituals, prayers and ceremonies associated with particular deities (''shosonbō'', 諸尊法) including the buddhas {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} and [[Amitābha|Amida]], the bodhisattvas [[Manjushri|Monju]], {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Kokuzo|1=Ākāśagarbha}} and [[Kannon|Kannon]] as well as Indian deities like [[Benzaiten|Benzai-ten]] and Japanese Kami like {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, and [[Daikokuten|Daikoku]]. ==Notable sites== The following are notable sites associated with Shugendo, many of which serve as popular pilgrimage destinations.{{cite web |url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/shugendou.html |title=Shugendo - Japanese Mountain Ascetism, Shamanism, En no Gyoja, Enno Gyoja, Esoteric Buddhism, Tendai, Shingon |work=Japanese Buddhist Statuary A to Z Photo Library: Dictionary of Gods, Goddesses, Shinto Kami, Creatures, and Demons |last=Schumacher |first=Mark |date=2015 |access-date=2023-07-23}} *{{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} 大峰山. Primary temple: Ominesan-ji Temple 大峰山寺 *[[Mount Kinpusen]] 金峯山, associated with the deity Zaō [[Gongen]] 金剛蔵王権現. Primary temple: [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple 金峯山寺 *{{ill|Mount Ishizuchi|en|Mount Ishizuchi|WD=Q2744214|lt=Ishizuchisan|1=Mount Ishizuchi}} 石鎚山. Associated with the deities Ishizuchi Kongo Zaō Dai Gongen [http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html 石鎚金剛蔵王大権現]{{Cite web |title=石鎚金剛蔵王大権現 |url=http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html |access-date=2024-05-14 |website=www.mandala88.jp}}''',''' a deity consisting of the Amida triad and Hōkibō Daitengu 法起坊大天狗. Primary temple: Gokurakuji 極楽寺, home of the [[:ja:極楽寺_(西条市)|Ishizuchisan Shingon Sect]]. *{{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Mount Haku|1=Mount Haku}}: Gozenpō 御前峰, Ōnanjimine 大汝峰, Bessan 別山, Kengamine 剣ヶ峰, Ōkurayama 大倉山, and Sannomine 三ノ峰 peaks (all of which are over 2,000 meters) *Sanyama-sama 三山様: the three mountains of [[:en:Dewa Sanzan|Dewa Sanzan]] 出羽三山 **{{ill|Mount Haguro|en|Mount Haguro|WD=Q3090765|lt=Mount Haguro|1=Mount Haguro}} 羽黒山 (419 meters), associated with Shō-Kannon Bodhisattva ([[:en:Avalokiteśvāra|Avalokiteśvāra]]) and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto ([[Uganomitama]]) 宇迦之御魂神. Primary temple: Hagurosan Kōtakuji Shōzenin 羽黒山荒沢寺正善院. The Haguro Autumn Peak Ritual (Akinomine 秋乃峰) is held there during the final week of August. **{{ill|Mount Gassan|en|Mount Gassan|WD=Q3174863|lt=Mount Gassan|1=Mount Gassan}} 月山 (1980 meters), associated with Amida Buddha ([[Amitābha]]) and Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto 月読命 **{{ill|Yudonosan Shrine|en|Yudonosan Shrine|WD=Q11563607|lt=Yudonosan Shrine|1=Yudonosan Shrine}} 湯殿山 (1504 meters), associated with Dainichi Buddha ([[Mahāvairocana]]) and Ōyamatsumi 大山津見神 (or 大山祇) *[[Mount Minō]] 箕面山 (near Osaka) in the [[Ikoma Mountains]] *[[Mount Izusan]] 伊豆山 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. Primary temple: [[Izusan Shrine]] 伊豆山神社 *{{ill|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|en|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|WD=Q11433560|lt=Mount Katsuragi|1=Mount Yamato Katsuragi}} 葛木 (between Nara and Osaka Prefectures) *Takisanji Temple 滝山寺 ({{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Sect) in {{ill|Okazaki, Aichi|en|Okazaki, Aichi|WD=Q242783|lt=Okazaki City|1=Okazaki, Aichi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}} *{{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake|WD=Q1754806|lt=Mount Ontake|1=Mount Ontake}} (also called Kiso Ontake, overlooking the Kiso Valley in {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}) *[[Mount Mitoku]] (Mitokusan) {{ill|Sanbutsu-ji|en|Sanbutsu-ji|WD=Q3471689|lt=Sanbutsu-ji|1=Sanbutsu-ji}} Temple 三徳山三仏寺 in {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|en|Tottori Prefecture|WD=Q133935|lt=Tottori Prefecture|1=Tottori Prefecture}} ==Gallery== File:Yamabushi-Omini-Okugakemichi-Yoshino.jpg|Yamabushi on the Ōmine Okugakemichi near Yoshino (Japan) File:Ascetic-Waterfall-Practice-Shipporyu-ji (Osaka Prefecture).jpg|Ascetic waterfall exercise supervised by a monk (Shippōryū-ji Temple) File:Yamabushi.jpg|Contemporary [[yamabushi]] File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi) Syugenja2.jpg|Mount Kongo (Kongosanchi) Syugenja == See also == * {{ill|Kaihōgyō|en|Kaihōgyō|WD=Q1330684|lt=Kaihōgyō|1=Kaihōgyō}} * {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|WD=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō|1=Mikkyō}} * {{ill|Milarepa|en|Milarepa|WD=Q58431|lt=Milarepa|1=Milarepa}} * [[Mount Hatsuka]] * [[Mount Hiei#Marathon monks|Mount Hiei]] * [[Mount Ōfuna]] * [[Mount Ōmine#Tests of courage|Mount Ōmine]] * [[Onmyōdō]] * {{ill|Sokushinbutsu|en|Sokushinbutsu|WD=Q285632|lt=Sokushinbutsu|1=Sokushinbutsu}} == Citations == {{reflist}} == General and cited references == {{refbegin}} * Andrea Castiglioni, Fabio Rambelli, & Carina Roth, eds. [[ca:Shugendo]][[cs:Šugendó]][[de:Shugendō]][[en:Shugendō]][[es:Shugendō]][[fr:Shugendō]][[it:Shugendō]][[ja:修験道]][[ko:수험도]][[pl:Shugendō]][[pt:Shugendō]][[ru:Сюгэндо]][[simple:Shugendō]][[sk:Šugendó]][[sr:Šugendo]][[tr:Shugendō]][[zh:修驗道]] [[ca:Shugendo]][[cs:Šugendó]][[de:Shugendō]][[en:Shugendō]][[es:Shugendō]][[fr:Shugendō]][[it:Shugendō]][[ja:修験道]][[ko:수험도]][[pl:Shugendō]][[pt:Shugendō]][[ru:Сюгэндо]][[simple:Shugendō]][[sk:Šugendó]][[sr:Šugendo]][[tr:Shugendō]][[zh:修驗道]] {{Short description|Syncretic religion from Heian Japan}} {{Italic title}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} [[Image:立石光正DSCF0451.JPG|thumb|''Shugendō ''practitioners (''Shugenja'') in the mountains of {{ill|Kumano, Mie|en|Kumano, Mie|WD=Q819672|lt=Kumano, Mie|1=Kumano, Mie}}]] [[File:En no Gyōja, Kamakura period, polychromed wood.JPG|thumb|upright|Statue of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of ''Shugendo''. {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, c. 1300–1375, {{ill|Kimbell Art Museum|en|Kimbell Art Museum|WD=Q1741629|lt=Kimbell Art Museum|1=Kimbell Art Museum}}.]] [[Image:Oominesanji stairs.jpg|thumb|upright|Stairs on the way to {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}}, the holy site of ''Shugendō''.]] [[Image:Fudō Myōō.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] silk scroll from [[Daigo-ji]] ({{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}), a major Shingon temple and Shugendō site.]] [[Image:Zao-Gongen-Kimpusen-Temple-Yoshino.jpg|thumb|upright|''Zaō Gongen'', a key deity in ''Shugendō'', in [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple.]] {{nihongo|'''''Shugendō'''''|||lit. the "Way [of] Trial [and] Practice", the "Way of ''Shugen'', or ''Gen''-practice"}} is a highly {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} religion,{{Cite journal |last=Sekimori |first=Gaynor |date=2009 |title=Defining Shugendō Past and Present: The "Restoration" of Shugendō at Nikkō and Koshikidake |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/asie_0766-1177_2009_num_18_1_1330 |journal=Cahiers d'Extrême-Asie |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=47–71 |doi=10.3406/asie.2009.1330}} a body of [[:en:Ascetic|Ascetic]] practices that originated in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period|1=Nara period}} of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}} having evolved during the 7th century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local [[Japanese folklore|folk-religious practices]], [[:en:Ko-shinto|Shinto]] {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} and [[Taoism]]. The final purpose of ''Shugendō'' is for practitioners to find supernatural power and save themselves and the masses by conducting religious training while treading through steep mountain ranges. Practitioners are called {{nihongo|''Shugenja''|}} or {{nihongo|''[[Yamabushi]]''|||literally "Mountain Prostrator"}}.{{Cite web|title=Exoteric Buddhism, Esoteric Buddhism, and Shugendo – 顕教・密教・修験道|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|url-status=live|website=www.tendai-jimon.jp|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}} The mountains where ''shugendo'' is practiced are all over Japan, and can span multiple mountains within one range such as the Ōmine mountain range with [[Mount Hakkyō]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} or the Ishizuchisan mountain range with [[:ja:%E7%93%B6%E3%83%B6%E6%A3%AE|Kamegamori]] and Tengudake. The ''Shugendō'' worldview includes a large pantheon of deities (which include Buddhist and Shinto figures). Some of the most important figures are the {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} figures of [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] and {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}}. Other key figures are {{nihongo|''[[Gongen]]''|}}, which are considered to be the manifestation of Buddhas as Japanese [[kami]]. {{nihongo|[[Zaō Gongen]]|}} is one of the most important gongen in ''Shugendō''.{{Cite web|title=修験道とは …「自然と人間」|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |title=The Formation and its Meaning of the 75-sacred-place View in the Omine Sacred Mountain Area |author=Masayasu Oda|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502160622/https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |accessdate=2 February 2021|archive-date=2 May 2019 }} == History == ''Shugendō'' evolved during the seventh century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local folk-religious practices, Shinto mountain worship and Buddhism.{{cite book|last1=Kornicki|first1=P.F.|last2=McMullen|first2=I. J.|title=Religion in Japan: Arrows to Heaven and Earth|date=1996|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0521550284|pages=13–|edition=Reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gsLDwvmnt_oC&pg=PA13|access-date=11 March 2017|language=en}} The seventh-century ascetic and mystic {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} is widely considered as the patriarch of ''Shugendō'', having first organized ''Shugendō'' as a doctrine. ''Shugendō'' literally means "the path of training and testing" or "the way to spiritual power through discipline."{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings|url=https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick|url-access=limited|date=1994|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Connecticut|isbn=0313264317|page=[https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick/page/n133 99]}}{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=Collected Writings of Carmen Blacker|date=2000|publisher=Japan Library|location=Richmond, Surrey|isbn=978-1873410929|pages=186–199|chapter=16: Initiation in the Shugendō: the Passage Through the Ten States of Existence}} ''Shugendō'' practitioners are also said to be descendants of the [[:en:Kōya Hijiri|Kōya Hijiri]] monks of the eighth and ninth centuries.{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|date=1999|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410859|edition=3rd|location=Richmond|pages=165–167}} From the ninth century, elements of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana Buddhism|1=Vajrayana}} such as {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} and {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Buddhism were taken into ''Shugendō'' and it developed further. In the Heian period, it became very popular among the nobles living in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to visit [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]] (three major shrines, [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]], [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] and [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]), which was the common holy place of ''Shugendō'', Shinto and Buddhism.{{Cite book|author=Makoto Satō, Fumihiko Gomi, Toshihiko Takano and Yasushi Toriumi|title=詳説日本史研究|year=2008|publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha Ltd.|isbn=978-4634011014}} The {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji|1=Meiji era}} government, which [[Shinbutsu bunri|erected a barrier between]] Shinto and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, ruled that ''Shugendō'' was unacceptable because of its amalgamation of the two religions, and officially forbade it in 1872. With the advent of {{ill|Freedom of religion in Japan|en|Freedom of religion in Japan|WD=Q5500773|lt=religious freedom in Japan|1=Freedom of religion in Japan}} after {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, ''Shugendō'' was revived.{{cite book|author=Catherine Cornille|title=The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Inter-Religious Dialogue|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHdgFhRKCOsC|year=2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1118529942}} In 1907, Yoshitaro Shibasaki and his team successfully climbed {{ill|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|en|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|WD=Q1109050|lt=Mount Tsurugi|1=Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)}}, which was regarded as the last unclimbed mountain in Japan. However, they found a metal cane decoration and a sword on the top of the mountain, and it turned out that someone had reached the top before them. A later scientific investigation revealed that the metal cane decoration and sword dated from the late Nara period to the early Heian period and that ''shugenja'' had climbed Mount Tsurugi more than 1,000 years ago.{{cite web|url=https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930190011/https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|script-title=ja:銅錫杖頭附鉄剣（剣岳発見）|language=ja|publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]], Government of Japan|archive-date=September 30, 2020}} The Ōmine mountain range, which stretches 100 km from north to south and connects {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} and [[Kumano Region|Kumano]], was historically the biggest practice place of ''Shugendō''. The highest peak of the Ōmine mountain range is [[Mount Hakkyō]] at an altitude of 1915 m, and there are 75 places for ascetic practices along the mountain trail, and {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}} Temple at the top of {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} at an altitude of 1719 m is considered to be the highest sacred site of ''Shugendō''. At present, the Ōmine mountain range is designated as a {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} {{ill|World Heritage Site|en|World Heritage Site|WD=Q9259|lt=World Heritage Site|1=World Heritage Site}} "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}" and {{ill|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|en|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|WD=Q1204533|lt=Yoshino-Kumano National Park|1=Yoshino-Kumano National Park}}. In modern times, ''Shugendō'' is practiced mainly through {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} and {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} temples. Some temples include {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kimpusen-ji|1=Kimpusen-ji}} in {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} (Tendai), Ideha Shrine in the {{ill|Three Mountains of Dewa|en|Three Mountains of Dewa|WD=Q1155726|lt=Three Mountains of Dewa|1=Three Mountains of Dewa}} and [[Daigo-ji]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} (Shingon). == Practices == According to Miyake Hitoshi, Shugend''ō'' rituals include "festivals, fortunetelling, divination, prayers and incantations, exorcism, spells, charms and so forth."Miyake Hitoshi. "Religious Rituals in Shugendo A Summary." ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 1989 16/2–3 Hitoshi describes the main worldview which informs Shugendo praxis as one which:
assumes the existence of at least two realms of existence, that of the daily lives of human beings, and a separate, supernatural spiritual realm behind, and which controls that of the daily lives of human beings. The mountains are seen either as a sacred space which is part of both of these worlds, or is seen to actually be a part of the spiritual world. The altar space during the fire ceremony, or the area of a matsuri, is also considered to be this kind of sacred space.
The {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} deity [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] (Sanskrit: Acala, "Immovable") plays a central role in the Shugendo cosmology practice. Another important Buddha is {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}} (大日如来，Mahavairocana). The Shugendo pantheon also includes numerous other Buddhist, Shinto and local religious figures. The most important Shugend''ō'' practices are "practices in the mountains" (''nyūbu shugyō'', 入峰修行). In Shugend''ō'', sacred mountains are seen as a supernatural home of numerous deities and as a symbol of the entire universe. According to Hitoshi, "the central element which forms both of these rituals is the symbolic action exhibited in a state of identification with the central deity Fudō Myōō." The main source of the shugenja's spiritual power generally understood to be Fudō Myōō and a shugenja gains the ability to use Fudō Myōō's power through mountain practices. There are three main forms of mountain practice according to Miyake Hitoshi: * "Entering the mountain to make offerings of flowers, read or bury sutras, and so forth, in honor of various buddhas or other deities, based on the belief that the mountain is a sacred area like a mandala." * "Entering the mountain for a certain period of time," a kind of mountain retreat during which yamabushi do various ascetic practices and receive esoteric knowledge and initiations. * The most severe and advanced ''nyūbu'' is the wintertime retreat in the mountains. This is said to confer special spiritual powers. Shugendō esoteric initiations are called ''shōkanjō'' (正灌頂) and are unique to Shugendō tradition (but are based on Vajrayana Buddhist {{ill|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|en|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|WD=Q3505394|lt=abhiseka|1=Empowerment (Vajrayana)}} ceremonies). Another important Shugendō practice is the demonstration of magical and spiritual powers (''genjutsu'', 験 術). Such displays may include fire walking, walking on swords, and entering boiling water. Yet another important religious practice in Shugendō is various rites or rituals of worship (''kuyōhō'', 供養法) which includes making offerings to Shugendō deities (such as Fudō Myōō and [[Gongen|Zaō Gongen]]) as well as the chanting of sutras. Shugendō practitioners also take part in [[Japanese festivals|Shinto festivals]] (matsuri, 祭) and make offerings to [[kami]]. Other practices which are part of Shugendō include the following: * {{ill|Fortune-telling|en|Fortune-telling|WD=Q8011595|lt=Fortunetelling|1=Fortune-telling}} and {{ill|Divination|en|Divination|WD=Q1043197|lt=Divination|1=Divination}} (''bokusen'') * obtaining {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=oracles|1=Oracle}} through {{ill|Mediumship|en|Mediumship|WD=Q25416928|lt=mediums|1=Mediumship}} (''fujutsu'') * obtaining oracles through mediums that have been possessed by a deity (''yori kitō'', 憑祈禱) * Fire ceremonies for averting misfortunes (''sokusai [[Homa (ritual)|goma]]''), usually focused around [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] * Using {{ill|Incantation|en|Incantation|WD=Q1999796|lt=incantations|1=Incantation}} (''kaji'') for a specific purpose * Spells and charms (''fuju, majinai''), used for healing, childbirth, protection and so on. These may be inscribed on {{ill|Amulet|en|Amulet|WD=Q131557|lt=amulets|1=Amulet}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism|1=Exorcism}} (''tsukimono otoshi'') for healing purposes Shugendo ritualists also practice different rituals, prayers and ceremonies associated with particular deities (''shosonbō'', 諸尊法) including the buddhas {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} and [[Amitābha|Amida]], the bodhisattvas [[Manjushri|Monju]], {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Kokuzo|1=Ākāśagarbha}} and [[Kannon|Kannon]] as well as Indian deities like [[Benzaiten|Benzai-ten]] and Japanese Kami like {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, and [[Daikokuten|Daikoku]]. ==Notable sites== The following are notable sites associated with Shugendo, many of which serve as popular pilgrimage destinations.{{cite web |url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/shugendou.html |title=Shugendo - Japanese Mountain Ascetism, Shamanism, En no Gyoja, Enno Gyoja, Esoteric Buddhism, Tendai, Shingon |work=Japanese Buddhist Statuary A to Z Photo Library: Dictionary of Gods, Goddesses, Shinto Kami, Creatures, and Demons |last=Schumacher |first=Mark |date=2015 |access-date=2023-07-23}} *{{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} 大峰山. Primary temple: Ominesan-ji Temple 大峰山寺 *[[Mount Kinpusen]] 金峯山, associated with the deity Zaō [[Gongen]] 金剛蔵王権現. Primary temple: [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple 金峯山寺 *{{ill|Mount Ishizuchi|en|Mount Ishizuchi|WD=Q2744214|lt=Ishizuchisan|1=Mount Ishizuchi}} 石鎚山. Associated with the deities Ishizuchi Kongo Zaō Dai Gongen [http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html 石鎚金剛蔵王大権現]{{Cite web |title=石鎚金剛蔵王大権現 |url=http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html |access-date=2024-05-14 |website=www.mandala88.jp}}''',''' a deity consisting of the Amida triad and Hōkibō Daitengu 法起坊大天狗. Primary temple: Gokurakuji 極楽寺, home of the [[:ja:極楽寺_(西条市)|Ishizuchisan Shingon Sect]]. *{{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Mount Haku|1=Mount Haku}}: Gozenpō 御前峰, Ōnanjimine 大汝峰, Bessan 別山, Kengamine 剣ヶ峰, Ōkurayama 大倉山, and Sannomine 三ノ峰 peaks (all of which are over 2,000 meters) *Sanyama-sama 三山様: the three mountains of [[:en:Dewa Sanzan|Dewa Sanzan]] 出羽三山 **{{ill|Mount Haguro|en|Mount Haguro|WD=Q3090765|lt=Mount Haguro|1=Mount Haguro}} 羽黒山 (419 meters), associated with Shō-Kannon Bodhisattva ([[:en:Avalokiteśvāra|Avalokiteśvāra]]) and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto ([[Uganomitama]]) 宇迦之御魂神. Primary temple: Hagurosan Kōtakuji Shōzenin 羽黒山荒沢寺正善院. The Haguro Autumn Peak Ritual (Akinomine 秋乃峰) is held there during the final week of August. **{{ill|Mount Gassan|en|Mount Gassan|WD=Q3174863|lt=Mount Gassan|1=Mount Gassan}} 月山 (1980 meters), associated with Amida Buddha ([[Amitābha]]) and Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto 月読命 **{{ill|Yudonosan Shrine|en|Yudonosan Shrine|WD=Q11563607|lt=Yudonosan Shrine|1=Yudonosan Shrine}} 湯殿山 (1504 meters), associated with Dainichi Buddha ([[Mahāvairocana]]) and Ōyamatsumi 大山津見神 (or 大山祇) *[[Mount Minō]] 箕面山 (near Osaka) in the [[Ikoma Mountains]] *[[Mount Izusan]] 伊豆山 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. Primary temple: [[Izusan Shrine]] 伊豆山神社 *{{ill|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|en|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|WD=Q11433560|lt=Mount Katsuragi|1=Mount Yamato Katsuragi}} 葛木 (between Nara and Osaka Prefectures) *Takisanji Temple 滝山寺 ({{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Sect) in {{ill|Okazaki, Aichi|en|Okazaki, Aichi|WD=Q242783|lt=Okazaki City|1=Okazaki, Aichi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}} *{{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake|WD=Q1754806|lt=Mount Ontake|1=Mount Ontake}} (also called Kiso Ontake, overlooking the Kiso Valley in {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}) *[[Mount Mitoku]] (Mitokusan) {{ill|Sanbutsu-ji|en|Sanbutsu-ji|WD=Q3471689|lt=Sanbutsu-ji|1=Sanbutsu-ji}} Temple 三徳山三仏寺 in {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|en|Tottori Prefecture|WD=Q133935|lt=Tottori Prefecture|1=Tottori Prefecture}} ==Gallery== File:Yamabushi-Omini-Okugakemichi-Yoshino.jpg|Yamabushi on the Ōmine Okugakemichi near Yoshino (Japan) File:Ascetic-Waterfall-Practice-Shipporyu-ji (Osaka Prefecture).jpg|Ascetic waterfall exercise supervised by a monk (Shippōryū-ji Temple) File:Yamabushi.jpg|Contemporary [[yamabushi]] File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi) Syugenja2.jpg|Mount Kongo (Kongosanchi) Syugenja == See also == * {{ill|Kaihōgyō|en|Kaihōgyō|WD=Q1330684|lt=Kaihōgyō|1=Kaihōgyō}} * {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|WD=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō|1=Mikkyō}} * {{ill|Milarepa|en|Milarepa|WD=Q58431|lt=Milarepa|1=Milarepa}} * [[Mount Hatsuka]] * [[Mount Hiei#Marathon monks|Mount Hiei]] * [[Mount Ōfuna]] * [[Mount Ōmine#Tests of courage|Mount Ōmine]] * [[Onmyōdō]] * {{ill|Sokushinbutsu|en|Sokushinbutsu|WD=Q285632|lt=Sokushinbutsu|1=Sokushinbutsu}} == Citations == {{reflist}} == General and cited references == {{refbegin}} * Andrea Castiglioni, Fabio Rambelli, & Carina Roth, eds. ''Defining Shugendō: critical studies on Japanese mountain religion''. London: Bloomsbury Academic, 2020. * {{cite book|last1=Faure|first1=Bernard|last2=Moerman|first2=Max|last3=Sekimori|first3=Gaynor|title=Shugendō: The History and Culture of a Japanese Religion|date=2011|publisher=Ecole française d'Extrême-Orient, centre de Kyoto|location=Kyoto|isbn=9782855391236}} * {{cite journal|last1=Gill|first1=Andrea K.|title=Shugendō: Pilgrimage and Ritual in {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}}, the holy site of ''Shugendō''.]] [[Image:Fudō Myōō.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] silk scroll from [[Daigo-ji]] ({{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}), a major Shingon temple and Shugendō site.]] [[Image:Zao-Gongen-Kimpusen-Temple-Yoshino.jpg|thumb|upright|''Zaō Gongen'', a key deity in ''Shugendō'', in [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple.]] {{nihongo|'''''Shugendō'''''|||lit. the "Way [of] Trial [and] Practice", the "Way of ''Shugen'', or ''Gen''-practice"}} is a highly {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} religion,{{Cite journal |last=Sekimori |first=Gaynor |date=2009 |title=Defining Shugendō Past and Present: The "Restoration" of Shugendō at Nikkō and Koshikidake |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/asie_0766-1177_2009_num_18_1_1330 |journal=Cahiers d'Extrême-Asie |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=47–71 |doi=10.3406/asie.2009.1330}} a body of [[:en:Ascetic|Ascetic]] practices that originated in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period|1=Nara period}} of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}} having evolved during the 7th century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local [[Japanese folklore|folk-religious practices]], [[:en:Ko-shinto|Shinto]] {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} and [[Taoism]]. The final purpose of ''Shugendō'' is for practitioners to find supernatural power and save themselves and the masses by conducting religious training while treading through steep mountain ranges. Practitioners are called {{nihongo|''Shugenja''|}} or {{nihongo|''[[Yamabushi]]''|||literally "Mountain Prostrator"}}.{{Cite web|title=Exoteric Buddhism, Esoteric Buddhism, and Shugendo – 顕教・密教・修験道|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|url-status=live|website=www.tendai-jimon.jp|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}} The mountains where ''shugendo'' is practiced are all over Japan, and can span multiple mountains within one range such as the Ōmine mountain range with [[Mount Hakkyō]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} or the Ishizuchisan mountain range with [[:ja:%E7%93%B6%E3%83%B6%E6%A3%AE|Kamegamori]] and Tengudake. The ''Shugendō'' worldview includes a large pantheon of deities (which include Buddhist and Shinto figures). Some of the most important figures are the {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} figures of [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] and {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}}. Other key figures are {{nihongo|''[[Gongen]]''|}}, which are considered to be the manifestation of Buddhas as Japanese [[kami]]. {{nihongo|[[Zaō Gongen]]|}} is one of the most important gongen in ''Shugendō''.{{Cite web|title=修験道とは …「自然と人間」|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |title=The Formation and its Meaning of the 75-sacred-place View in the Omine Sacred Mountain Area |author=Masayasu Oda|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502160622/https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |accessdate=2 February 2021|archive-date=2 May 2019 }} == History == ''Shugendō'' evolved during the seventh century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local folk-religious practices, Shinto mountain worship and Buddhism.{{cite book|last1=Kornicki|first1=P.F.|last2=McMullen|first2=I. J.|title=Religion in Japan: Arrows to Heaven and Earth|date=1996|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0521550284|pages=13–|edition=Reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gsLDwvmnt_oC&pg=PA13|access-date=11 March 2017|language=en}} The seventh-century ascetic and mystic {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} is widely considered as the patriarch of ''Shugendō'', having first organized ''Shugendō'' as a doctrine. ''Shugendō'' literally means "the path of training and testing" or "the way to spiritual power through discipline."{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings|url=https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick|url-access=limited|date=1994|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Connecticut|isbn=0313264317|page=[https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick/page/n133 99]}}{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=Collected Writings of Carmen Blacker|date=2000|publisher=Japan Library|location=Richmond, Surrey|isbn=978-1873410929|pages=186–199|chapter=16: Initiation in the Shugendō: the Passage Through the Ten States of Existence}} ''Shugendō'' practitioners are also said to be descendants of the [[:en:Kōya Hijiri|Kōya Hijiri]] monks of the eighth and ninth centuries.{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|date=1999|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410859|edition=3rd|location=Richmond|pages=165–167}} From the ninth century, elements of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana Buddhism|1=Vajrayana}} such as {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} and {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Buddhism were taken into ''Shugendō'' and it developed further. In the Heian period, it became very popular among the nobles living in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to visit [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]] (three major shrines, [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]], [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] and [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]), which was the common holy place of ''Shugendō'', Shinto and Buddhism.{{Cite book|author=Makoto Satō, Fumihiko Gomi, Toshihiko Takano and Yasushi Toriumi|title=詳説日本史研究|year=2008|publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha Ltd.|isbn=978-4634011014}} The {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji|1=Meiji era}} government, which [[Shinbutsu bunri|erected a barrier between]] Shinto and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, ruled that ''Shugendō'' was unacceptable because of its amalgamation of the two religions, and officially forbade it in 1872. With the advent of {{ill|Freedom of religion in Japan|en|Freedom of religion in Japan|WD=Q5500773|lt=religious freedom in Japan|1=Freedom of religion in Japan}} after {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, ''Shugendō'' was revived.{{cite book|author=Catherine Cornille|title=The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Inter-Religious Dialogue|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHdgFhRKCOsC|year=2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1118529942}} In 1907, Yoshitaro Shibasaki and his team successfully climbed {{ill|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|en|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|WD=Q1109050|lt=Mount Tsurugi|1=Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)}}, which was regarded as the last unclimbed mountain in Japan. However, they found a metal cane decoration and a sword on the top of the mountain, and it turned out that someone had reached the top before them. A later scientific investigation revealed that the metal cane decoration and sword dated from the late Nara period to the early Heian period and that ''shugenja'' had climbed Mount Tsurugi more than 1,000 years ago.{{cite web|url=https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930190011/https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|script-title=ja:銅錫杖頭附鉄剣（剣岳発見）|language=ja|publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]], Government of Japan|archive-date=September 30, 2020}} The Ōmine mountain range, which stretches 100 km from north to south and connects {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} and [[Kumano Region|Kumano]], was historically the biggest practice place of ''Shugendō''. The highest peak of the Ōmine mountain range is [[Mount Hakkyō]] at an altitude of 1915 m, and there are 75 places for ascetic practices along the mountain trail, and {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}} Temple at the top of {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} at an altitude of 1719 m is considered to be the highest sacred site of ''Shugendō''. At present, the Ōmine mountain range is designated as a {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} {{ill|World Heritage Site|en|World Heritage Site|WD=Q9259|lt=World Heritage Site|1=World Heritage Site}} "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}" and {{ill|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|en|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|WD=Q1204533|lt=Yoshino-Kumano National Park|1=Yoshino-Kumano National Park}}. In modern times, ''Shugendō'' is practiced mainly through {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} and {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} temples. Some temples include {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kimpusen-ji|1=Kimpusen-ji}} in {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} (Tendai), Ideha Shrine in the {{ill|Three Mountains of Dewa|en|Three Mountains of Dewa|WD=Q1155726|lt=Three Mountains of Dewa|1=Three Mountains of Dewa}} and [[Daigo-ji]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} (Shingon). == Practices == According to Miyake Hitoshi, Shugend''ō'' rituals include "festivals, fortunetelling, divination, prayers and incantations, exorcism, spells, charms and so forth."Miyake Hitoshi. "Religious Rituals in Shugendo A Summary." ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 1989 16/2–3 Hitoshi describes the main worldview which informs Shugendo praxis as one which:
assumes the existence of at least two realms of existence, that of the daily lives of human beings, and a separate, supernatural spiritual realm behind, and which controls that of the daily lives of human beings. The mountains are seen either as a sacred space which is part of both of these worlds, or is seen to actually be a part of the spiritual world. The altar space during the fire ceremony, or the area of a matsuri, is also considered to be this kind of sacred space.
The {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} deity [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] (Sanskrit: Acala, "Immovable") plays a central role in the Shugendo cosmology practice. Another important Buddha is {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}} (大日如来，Mahavairocana). The Shugendo pantheon also includes numerous other Buddhist, Shinto and local religious figures. The most important Shugend''ō'' practices are "practices in the mountains" (''nyūbu shugyō'', 入峰修行). In Shugend''ō'', sacred mountains are seen as a supernatural home of numerous deities and as a symbol of the entire universe. According to Hitoshi, "the central element which forms both of these rituals is the symbolic action exhibited in a state of identification with the central deity Fudō Myōō." The main source of the shugenja's spiritual power generally understood to be Fudō Myōō and a shugenja gains the ability to use Fudō Myōō's power through mountain practices. There are three main forms of mountain practice according to Miyake Hitoshi: * "Entering the mountain to make offerings of flowers, read or bury sutras, and so forth, in honor of various buddhas or other deities, based on the belief that the mountain is a sacred area like a mandala." * "Entering the mountain for a certain period of time," a kind of mountain retreat during which yamabushi do various ascetic practices and receive esoteric knowledge and initiations. * The most severe and advanced ''nyūbu'' is the wintertime retreat in the mountains. This is said to confer special spiritual powers. Shugendō esoteric initiations are called ''shōkanjō'' (正灌頂) and are unique to Shugendō tradition (but are based on Vajrayana Buddhist {{ill|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|en|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|WD=Q3505394|lt=abhiseka|1=Empowerment (Vajrayana)}} ceremonies). Another important Shugendō practice is the demonstration of magical and spiritual powers (''genjutsu'', 験 術). Such displays may include fire walking, walking on swords, and entering boiling water. Yet another important religious practice in Shugendō is various rites or rituals of worship (''kuyōhō'', 供養法) which includes making offerings to Shugendō deities (such as Fudō Myōō and [[Gongen|Zaō Gongen]]) as well as the chanting of sutras. Shugendō practitioners also take part in [[Japanese festivals|Shinto festivals]] (matsuri, 祭) and make offerings to [[kami]]. Other practices which are part of Shugendō include the following: * {{ill|Fortune-telling|en|Fortune-telling|WD=Q8011595|lt=Fortunetelling|1=Fortune-telling}} and {{ill|Divination|en|Divination|WD=Q1043197|lt=Divination|1=Divination}} (''bokusen'') * obtaining {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=oracles|1=Oracle}} through {{ill|Mediumship|en|Mediumship|WD=Q25416928|lt=mediums|1=Mediumship}} (''fujutsu'') * obtaining oracles through mediums that have been possessed by a deity (''yori kitō'', 憑祈禱) * Fire ceremonies for averting misfortunes (''sokusai [[Homa (ritual)|goma]]''), usually focused around [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] * Using {{ill|Incantation|en|Incantation|WD=Q1999796|lt=incantations|1=Incantation}} (''kaji'') for a specific purpose * Spells and charms (''fuju, majinai''), used for healing, childbirth, protection and so on. These may be inscribed on {{ill|Amulet|en|Amulet|WD=Q131557|lt=amulets|1=Amulet}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism|1=Exorcism}} (''tsukimono otoshi'') for healing purposes Shugendo ritualists also practice different rituals, prayers and ceremonies associated with particular deities (''shosonbō'', 諸尊法) including the buddhas {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} and [[Amitābha|Amida]], the bodhisattvas [[Manjushri|Monju]], {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Kokuzo|1=Ākāśagarbha}} and [[Kannon|Kannon]] as well as Indian deities like [[Benzaiten|Benzai-ten]] and Japanese Kami like {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, and [[Daikokuten|Daikoku]]. ==Notable sites== The following are notable sites associated with Shugendo, many of which serve as popular pilgrimage destinations.{{cite web |url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/shugendou.html |title=Shugendo - Japanese Mountain Ascetism, Shamanism, En no Gyoja, Enno Gyoja, Esoteric Buddhism, Tendai, Shingon |work=Japanese Buddhist Statuary A to Z Photo Library: Dictionary of Gods, Goddesses, Shinto Kami, Creatures, and Demons |last=Schumacher |first=Mark |date=2015 |access-date=2023-07-23}} *{{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} 大峰山. Primary temple: Ominesan-ji Temple 大峰山寺 *[[Mount Kinpusen]] 金峯山, associated with the deity Zaō [[Gongen]] 金剛蔵王権現. Primary temple: [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple 金峯山寺 *{{ill|Mount Ishizuchi|en|Mount Ishizuchi|WD=Q2744214|lt=Ishizuchisan|1=Mount Ishizuchi}} 石鎚山. Associated with the deities Ishizuchi Kongo Zaō Dai Gongen [http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html 石鎚金剛蔵王大権現]{{Cite web |title=石鎚金剛蔵王大権現 |url=http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html |access-date=2024-05-14 |website=www.mandala88.jp}}''',''' a deity consisting of the Amida triad and Hōkibō Daitengu 法起坊大天狗. Primary temple: Gokurakuji 極楽寺, home of the [[:ja:極楽寺_(西条市)|Ishizuchisan Shingon Sect]]. *{{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Mount Haku|1=Mount Haku}}: Gozenpō 御前峰, Ōnanjimine 大汝峰, Bessan 別山, Kengamine 剣ヶ峰, Ōkurayama 大倉山, and Sannomine 三ノ峰 peaks (all of which are over 2,000 meters) *Sanyama-sama 三山様: the three mountains of [[:en:Dewa Sanzan|Dewa Sanzan]] 出羽三山 **{{ill|Mount Haguro|en|Mount Haguro|WD=Q3090765|lt=Mount Haguro|1=Mount Haguro}} 羽黒山 (419 meters), associated with Shō-Kannon Bodhisattva ([[:en:Avalokiteśvāra|Avalokiteśvāra]]) and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto ([[Uganomitama]]) 宇迦之御魂神. Primary temple: Hagurosan Kōtakuji Shōzenin 羽黒山荒沢寺正善院. The Haguro Autumn Peak Ritual (Akinomine 秋乃峰) is held there during the final week of August. **{{ill|Mount Gassan|en|Mount Gassan|WD=Q3174863|lt=Mount Gassan|1=Mount Gassan}} 月山 (1980 meters), associated with Amida Buddha ([[Amitābha]]) and Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto 月読命 **{{ill|Yudonosan Shrine|en|Yudonosan Shrine|WD=Q11563607|lt=Yudonosan Shrine|1=Yudonosan Shrine}} 湯殿山 (1504 meters), associated with Dainichi Buddha ([[Mahāvairocana]]) and Ōyamatsumi 大山津見神 (or 大山祇) *[[Mount Minō]] 箕面山 (near Osaka) in the [[Ikoma Mountains]] *[[Mount Izusan]] 伊豆山 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. Primary temple: [[Izusan Shrine]] 伊豆山神社 *{{ill|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|en|Mount Yamato Katsuragi|WD=Q11433560|lt=Mount Katsuragi|1=Mount Yamato Katsuragi}} 葛木 (between Nara and Osaka Prefectures) *Takisanji Temple 滝山寺 ({{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Sect) in {{ill|Okazaki, Aichi|en|Okazaki, Aichi|WD=Q242783|lt=Okazaki City|1=Okazaki, Aichi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}} *{{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake|WD=Q1754806|lt=Mount Ontake|1=Mount Ontake}} (also called Kiso Ontake, overlooking the Kiso Valley in {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}) *[[Mount Mitoku]] (Mitokusan) {{ill|Sanbutsu-ji|en|Sanbutsu-ji|WD=Q3471689|lt=Sanbutsu-ji|1=Sanbutsu-ji}} Temple 三徳山三仏寺 in {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|en|Tottori Prefecture|WD=Q133935|lt=Tottori Prefecture|1=Tottori Prefecture}} ==Gallery== File:Yamabushi-Omini-Okugakemichi-Yoshino.jpg|Yamabushi on the Ōmine Okugakemichi near Yoshino (Japan) File:Ascetic-Waterfall-Practice-Shipporyu-ji (Osaka Prefecture).jpg|Ascetic waterfall exercise supervised by a monk (Shippōryū-ji Temple) File:Yamabushi.jpg|Contemporary [[yamabushi]] File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi) Syugenja2.jpg|Mount Kongo (Kongosanchi) Syugenja == See also == * {{ill|Kaihōgyō|en|Kaihōgyō|WD=Q1330684|lt=Kaihōgyō|1=Kaihōgyō}} * {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|WD=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō|1=Mikkyō}} * {{ill|Milarepa|en|Milarepa|WD=Q58431|lt=Milarepa|1=Milarepa}} * [[Mount Hatsuka]] * [[Mount Hiei#Marathon monks|Mount Hiei]] * [[Mount Ōfuna]] * [[Mount Ōmine#Tests of courage|Mount Ōmine]] * [[Onmyōdō]] * {{ill|Sokushinbutsu|en|Sokushinbutsu|WD=Q285632|lt=Sokushinbutsu|1=Sokushinbutsu}} == Citations == {{reflist}} == General and cited references == {{refbegin}} * Andrea Castiglioni, Fabio Rambelli, & Carina Roth, eds. {{Short description|Syncretic religion from Heian Japan}} {{Italic title}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} [[Image:立石光正DSCF0451.JPG|thumb|''Shugendō ''practitioners (''Shugenja'') in the mountains of {{ill|Kumano, Mie|en|Kumano, Mie|WD=Q819672|lt=Kumano, Mie|1=Kumano, Mie}}]] [[File:En no Gyōja, Kamakura period, polychromed wood.JPG|thumb|upright|Statue of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of ''Shugendo''. {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, c. 1300–1375, {{ill|Kimbell Art Museum|en|Kimbell Art Museum|WD=Q1741629|lt=Kimbell Art Museum|1=Kimbell Art Museum}}.]] [[Image:Oominesanji stairs.jpg|thumb|upright|Stairs on the way to {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}}, the holy site of ''Shugendō''.]] [[Image:Fudō Myōō.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] silk scroll from [[Daigo-ji]] ({{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}), a major Shingon temple and Shugendō site.]] [[Image:Zao-Gongen-Kimpusen-Temple-Yoshino.jpg|thumb|upright|''Zaō Gongen'', a key deity in ''Shugendō'', in [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple.]] {{nihongo|'''''Shugendō'''''|||lit. the "Way [of] Trial [and] Practice", the "Way of ''Shugen'', or ''Gen''-practice"}} is a highly {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} religion,{{Cite journal |last=Sekimori |first=Gaynor |date=2009 |title=Defining Shugendō Past and Present: The "Restoration" of Shugendō at Nikkō and Koshikidake |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/asie_0766-1177_2009_num_18_1_1330 |journal=Cahiers d'Extrême-Asie |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=47–71 |doi=10.3406/asie.2009.1330}} a body of [[:en:Ascetic|Ascetic]] practices that originated in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period|1=Nara period}} of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}} having evolved during the 7th century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local [[Japanese folklore|folk-religious practices]], [[:en:Ko-shinto|Shinto]] {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} and [[Taoism]]. The final purpose of ''Shugendō'' is for practitioners to find supernatural power and save themselves and the masses by conducting religious training while treading through steep mountain ranges. Practitioners are called {{nihongo|''Shugenja''|}} or {{nihongo|''[[Yamabushi]]''|||literally "Mountain Prostrator"}}.{{Cite web|title=Exoteric Buddhism, Esoteric Buddhism, and Shugendo – 顕教・密教・修験道|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|url-status=live|website=www.tendai-jimon.jp|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}} The mountains where ''shugendo'' is practiced are all over Japan, and can span multiple mountains within one range such as the Ōmine mountain range with [[Mount Hakkyō]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} or the Ishizuchisan mountain range with [[:ja:%E7%93%B6%E3%83%B6%E6%A3%AE|Kamegamori]] and Tengudake. The ''Shugendō'' worldview includes a large pantheon of deities (which include Buddhist and Shinto figures). Some of the most important figures are the {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} figures of [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] and {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}}. Other key figures are {{nihongo|''[[Gongen]]''|}}, which are considered to be the manifestation of Buddhas as Japanese [[kami]]. {{nihongo|[[Zaō Gongen]]|}} is one of the most important gongen in ''Shugendō''.{{Cite web|title=修験道とは …「自然と人間」|url=http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|publisher=Tendaijimon Sect|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221152905/http://www.tendai-jimon.jp/trainee/index.html|accessdate=31 January 2021|archive-date=21 December 2020}}{{Cite web |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |title=The Formation and its Meaning of the 75-sacred-place View in the Omine Sacred Mountain Area |author=Masayasu Oda|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502160622/https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjhg1948/41/6/41_6_512/_pdf |accessdate=2 February 2021|archive-date=2 May 2019 }} == History == ''Shugendō'' evolved during the seventh century from an amalgamation of beliefs, philosophies, doctrines and ritual systems drawn from local folk-religious practices, Shinto mountain worship and Buddhism.{{cite book|last1=Kornicki|first1=P.F.|last2=McMullen|first2=I. J.|title=Religion in Japan: Arrows to Heaven and Earth|date=1996|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0521550284|pages=13–|edition=Reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gsLDwvmnt_oC&pg=PA13|access-date=11 March 2017|language=en}} The seventh-century ascetic and mystic {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} is widely considered as the patriarch of ''Shugendō'', having first organized ''Shugendō'' as a doctrine. ''Shugendō'' literally means "the path of training and testing" or "the way to spiritual power through discipline."{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings|url=https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick|url-access=limited|date=1994|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Connecticut|isbn=0313264317|page=[https://archive.org/details/essentialsshinto00pick/page/n133 99]}}{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=Collected Writings of Carmen Blacker|date=2000|publisher=Japan Library|location=Richmond, Surrey|isbn=978-1873410929|pages=186–199|chapter=16: Initiation in the Shugendō: the Passage Through the Ten States of Existence}} ''Shugendō'' practitioners are also said to be descendants of the [[:en:Kōya Hijiri|Kōya Hijiri]] monks of the eighth and ninth centuries.{{cite book|last1=Blacker|first1=Carmen|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|date=1999|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410859|edition=3rd|location=Richmond|pages=165–167}} From the ninth century, elements of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana Buddhism|1=Vajrayana}} such as {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} and {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} Buddhism were taken into ''Shugendō'' and it developed further. In the Heian period, it became very popular among the nobles living in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to visit [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]] (three major shrines, [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]], [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] and [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]), which was the common holy place of ''Shugendō'', Shinto and Buddhism.{{Cite book|author=Makoto Satō, Fumihiko Gomi, Toshihiko Takano and Yasushi Toriumi|title=詳説日本史研究|year=2008|publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha Ltd.|isbn=978-4634011014}} The {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji|1=Meiji era}} government, which [[Shinbutsu bunri|erected a barrier between]] Shinto and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, ruled that ''Shugendō'' was unacceptable because of its amalgamation of the two religions, and officially forbade it in 1872. With the advent of {{ill|Freedom of religion in Japan|en|Freedom of religion in Japan|WD=Q5500773|lt=religious freedom in Japan|1=Freedom of religion in Japan}} after {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, ''Shugendō'' was revived.{{cite book|author=Catherine Cornille|title=The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Inter-Religious Dialogue|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHdgFhRKCOsC|year=2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1118529942}} In 1907, Yoshitaro Shibasaki and his team successfully climbed {{ill|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|en|Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|WD=Q1109050|lt=Mount Tsurugi|1=Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)}}, which was regarded as the last unclimbed mountain in Japan. However, they found a metal cane decoration and a sword on the top of the mountain, and it turned out that someone had reached the top before them. A later scientific investigation revealed that the metal cane decoration and sword dated from the late Nara period to the early Heian period and that ''shugenja'' had climbed Mount Tsurugi more than 1,000 years ago.{{cite web|url=https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930190011/https://toyama-bunkaisan.jp/search/1578/|script-title=ja:銅錫杖頭附鉄剣（剣岳発見）|language=ja|publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]], Government of Japan|archive-date=September 30, 2020}} The Ōmine mountain range, which stretches 100 km from north to south and connects {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} and [[Kumano Region|Kumano]], was historically the biggest practice place of ''Shugendō''. The highest peak of the Ōmine mountain range is [[Mount Hakkyō]] at an altitude of 1915 m, and there are 75 places for ascetic practices along the mountain trail, and {{ill|Ōminesan-ji|en|Ōminesan-ji|WD=Q3077344|lt=Ōminesan-ji|1=Ōminesan-ji}} Temple at the top of {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} at an altitude of 1719 m is considered to be the highest sacred site of ''Shugendō''. At present, the Ōmine mountain range is designated as a {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} {{ill|World Heritage Site|en|World Heritage Site|WD=Q9259|lt=World Heritage Site|1=World Heritage Site}} "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}" and {{ill|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|en|Yoshino-Kumano National Park|WD=Q1204533|lt=Yoshino-Kumano National Park|1=Yoshino-Kumano National Park}}. In modern times, ''Shugendō'' is practiced mainly through {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai|1=Tendai}} and {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon|1=Shingon Buddhism}} temples. Some temples include {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kimpusen-ji|1=Kimpusen-ji}} in {{ill|Yoshino District, Nara|en|Yoshino District, Nara|WD=Q1154558|lt=Yoshino|1=Yoshino District, Nara}} (Tendai), Ideha Shrine in the {{ill|Three Mountains of Dewa|en|Three Mountains of Dewa|WD=Q1155726|lt=Three Mountains of Dewa|1=Three Mountains of Dewa}} and [[Daigo-ji]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} (Shingon). == Practices == According to Miyake Hitoshi, Shugend''ō'' rituals include "festivals, fortunetelling, divination, prayers and incantations, exorcism, spells, charms and so forth."Miyake Hitoshi. "Religious Rituals in Shugendo A Summary." ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 1989 16/2–3 Hitoshi describes the main worldview which informs Shugendo praxis as one which:
assumes the existence of at least two realms of existence, that of the daily lives of human beings, and a separate, supernatural spiritual realm behind, and which controls that of the daily lives of human beings. The mountains are seen either as a sacred space which is part of both of these worlds, or is seen to actually be a part of the spiritual world. The altar space during the fire ceremony, or the area of a matsuri, is also considered to be this kind of sacred space.
The {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric Buddhist|1=Vajrayana}} deity [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] (Sanskrit: Acala, "Immovable") plays a central role in the Shugendo cosmology practice. Another important Buddha is {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai|1=Vairocana}} (大日如来，Mahavairocana). The Shugendo pantheon also includes numerous other Buddhist, Shinto and local religious figures. The most important Shugend''ō'' practices are "practices in the mountains" (''nyūbu shugyō'', 入峰修行). In Shugend''ō'', sacred mountains are seen as a supernatural home of numerous deities and as a symbol of the entire universe. According to Hitoshi, "the central element which forms both of these rituals is the symbolic action exhibited in a state of identification with the central deity Fudō Myōō." The main source of the shugenja's spiritual power generally understood to be Fudō Myōō and a shugenja gains the ability to use Fudō Myōō's power through mountain practices. There are three main forms of mountain practice according to Miyake Hitoshi: * "Entering the mountain to make offerings of flowers, read or bury sutras, and so forth, in honor of various buddhas or other deities, based on the belief that the mountain is a sacred area like a mandala." * "Entering the mountain for a certain period of time," a kind of mountain retreat during which yamabushi do various ascetic practices and receive esoteric knowledge and initiations. * The most severe and advanced ''nyūbu'' is the wintertime retreat in the mountains. This is said to confer special spiritual powers. Shugendō esoteric initiations are called ''shōkanjō'' (正灌頂) and are unique to Shugendō tradition (but are based on Vajrayana Buddhist {{ill|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|en|Empowerment (Vajrayana)|WD=Q3505394|lt=abhiseka|1=Empowerment (Vajrayana)}} ceremonies). Another important Shugendō practice is the demonstration of magical and spiritual powers (''genjutsu'', 験 術). Such displays may include fire walking, walking on swords, and entering boiling water. Yet another important religious practice in Shugendō is various rites or rituals of worship (''kuyōhō'', 供養法) which includes making offerings to Shugendō deities (such as Fudō Myōō and [[Gongen|Zaō Gongen]]) as well as the chanting of sutras. Shugendō practitioners also take part in [[Japanese festivals|Shinto festivals]] (matsuri, 祭) and make offerings to [[kami]]. Other practices which are part of Shugendō include the following: * {{ill|Fortune-telling|en|Fortune-telling|WD=Q8011595|lt=Fortunetelling|1=Fortune-telling}} and {{ill|Divination|en|Divination|WD=Q1043197|lt=Divination|1=Divination}} (''bokusen'') * obtaining {{ill|Oracle|en|Oracle|WD=Q217123|lt=oracles|1=Oracle}} through {{ill|Mediumship|en|Mediumship|WD=Q25416928|lt=mediums|1=Mediumship}} (''fujutsu'') * obtaining oracles through mediums that have been possessed by a deity (''yori kitō'', 憑祈禱) * Fire ceremonies for averting misfortunes (''sokusai [[Homa (ritual)|goma]]''), usually focused around [[Acala|Fudō Myōō]] * Using {{ill|Incantation|en|Incantation|WD=Q1999796|lt=incantations|1=Incantation}} (''kaji'') for a specific purpose * Spells and charms (''fuju, majinai''), used for healing, childbirth, protection and so on. These may be inscribed on {{ill|Amulet|en|Amulet|WD=Q131557|lt=amulets|1=Amulet}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism|1=Exorcism}} (''tsukimono otoshi'') for healing purposes Shugendo ritualists also practice different rituals, prayers and ceremonies associated with particular deities (''shosonbō'', 諸尊法) including the buddhas {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} and [[Amitābha|Amida]], the bodhisattvas [[Manjushri|Monju]], {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Kokuzo|1=Ākāśagarbha}} and [[Kannon|Kannon]] as well as Indian deities like [[Benzaiten|Benzai-ten]] and Japanese Kami like {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, and [[Daikokuten|Daikoku]]. ==Notable sites== The following are notable sites associated with Shugendo, many of which serve as popular pilgrimage destinations.{{cite web |url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/shugendou.html |title=Shugendo - Japanese Mountain Ascetism, Shamanism, En no Gyoja, Enno Gyoja, Esoteric Buddhism, Tendai, Shingon |work=Japanese Buddhist Statuary A to Z Photo Library: Dictionary of Gods, Goddesses, Shinto Kami, Creatures, and Demons |last=Schumacher |first=Mark |date=2015 |access-date=2023-07-23}} *{{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} 大峰山. Primary temple: Ominesan-ji Temple 大峰山寺 *[[Mount Kinpusen]] 金峯山, associated with the deity Zaō [[Gongen]] 金剛蔵王権現. Primary temple: [[:en:Kinpusen-ji|Kinpusen-ji]] Temple 金峯山寺 *{{ill|Mount Ishizuchi|en|Mount Ishizuchi|WD=Q2744214|lt=Ishizuchisan|1=Mount Ishizuchi}} 石鎚山. Associated with the deities Ishizuchi Kongo Zaō Dai Gongen [http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html 石鎚金剛蔵王大権現]{{Cite web |title=石鎚金剛蔵王大権現 |url=http://www.mandala88.jp/gokurakuji/rekishi/ishizuchi.html |access-date=2024-05-14 |website=www.mandala88.jp}}''',''' a deity consisting of the Amida triad and Hōkibō Daitengu 法起坊大天狗. Primary temple: Gokurakuji 極楽寺, home of the [[:ja:極楽寺_(西条市)|Ishizuchisan Shingon Sect]]. *{{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Mount Haku|1=Mount Haku}}: Gozenpō 御前峰, Ōnanjimine 大汝峰, Bessan 別山, Kengamine 剣ヶ峰, Ōkurayama 大倉山, and Sannomine 三ノ峰 peaks (all of which are over 2,000 meters) *Sanyama-sama 三山様: the three mountains of [[:en:Dewa Sanzan|Dewa Sanzan]] 出羽三山 **{{ill|Mount Haguro|en|Mount Haguro|WD=Q3090765|lt=Mount Haguro|1=Mount Haguro}} 羽黒山 (419 meters), associated with Shō-Kannon Bodhisattva ([[:en:Avalokiteśvāra|Avalokiteśvāra]]) and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto ([[Uganomitama]]) 宇迦之御魂神. Primary temple: Hagurosan Kōtakuji Shōzenin 羽黒山荒沢寺正善院. The Haguro Autumn Peak Ritual (Akinomine 秋乃峰) is held there during the final week of August. **{{ill|Mount Gassan|en|Mount Gassan|WD=Q3174863|lt=Mount Gassan|1=Mount Gassan}} 月山 (1980 meters), associated with Amida Buddha ([[Amitābha]]) and Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto 月読命 **{{ill|Yudonosan Shrine|en|Yudonosan Shrine|WD=Q11563607|lt=Yudonosan Shrine|1=Yudonosan Shrine}} 湯殿山 (1504 meters), associated with Dainichi Buddha ([[Mahāvairocana]]) and Ōyamatsumi 大山津見神 (or 大山祇) *[[Mount Minō]] 箕面山 (near Osaka) in the [[Ikoma Mountains]] *[[Mount Izusan]] 伊豆山 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}.
